{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2020}}
[[File:Tippies-of-1796-caricature.jpg|thumb|right|1796 fashion caricature by [[Richard Newton (caricaturist)|Richard Newton]]: the period's fashions of tight trousers for men, and one or two feathers in a woman's headdress, are both parodied through exaggeration.]]
{{Wiktionary|exaggeration}}

'''Exaggeration''' is the representation of something as more extreme or dramatic than it is, intentionally or unintentionally. It can be a [[rhetorical device]] or [[figure of speech]], used to evoke strong feelings or to create a strong impression. 

Amplifying achievements, obstacles and problems to [[attention seeking|seek attention]] is an everyday occurrence.<ref>Daniel Goleman, ''Emotional Intelligence'' (London 1996) p. 113.</ref> Inflating the difficulty of achieving a goal after attaining it, can be used to bolster [[self-esteem]].<ref>Beth Azar [https://www.apa.org/monitor/jun07/sciencewatch.aspx "All puffed up"] ''Monitor on Psychology'', June 2007, Vol 38, No. 6.</ref>

In the arts, exaggerations are used to create emphasis or effect. As a [[literary device]], exaggerations are often used in [[poetry]], and is frequently encountered in casual speech.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://literarydevices.net/hyperbole/ | title=Definition of Hyperbole | accessdate=10 January 2014}}</ref> Many times the usages of hyperbole describe something as better or worse than it really is.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hyperbole|title=Definition of HYPERBOLE|website=www.merriam-webster.com|date=7 May 2024 }}</ref> An example of hyperbole is: "The bag weighed a ton."<ref>{{cite book|last=Mahony|first=David|title=Literacy Tests Year 7|year=2003|publisher=Pascal Press|isbn=978-1877085369|page=82}}</ref> Hyperbole makes the point that the bag was very heavy, though it probably does not weigh a ton.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://rhetoric.byu.edu/figures/H/hyperbole.htm | title=Hyperbole | publisher=Byu.edu | accessdate=10 January 2014}}</ref>

Exaggerating is also a type of [[Deception#Types|deception]],<ref name="Guerrero, Andersen, & Afifi, 2007">Guerrero, L., Anderson, P., Afifi, W. (2007). Close Encounters: Communication in Relationships (2nd ed.). Los Angeles: Sage Publications.</ref> as well as a means of malingering – magnifying small injuries or discomforts as an excuse to [[malingering|avoid responsibilities]].<ref name=Rogers3>R. Rogers ''Clinical Assessment of Malingering and Deception'' 3rd Edition, Guilford, 2008. {{ISBN|1593856997}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The word has origins in the mid-16th century: from Latin exaggerat- 'heaped up', from the verb exaggerare, from ex- 'thoroughly' + aggerare 'heap up' (from agger 'heap'). The word originally meant 'pile up, accumulate', later 'intensify praise or blame', giving rise to current senses.

==In the arts==

The exaggerator has been a familiar figure in Western culture since at least [[Aristotle]]'s discussion of the [[alazon]].<ref>Aristotle, ''Ethics'' (Penguin 1976) p. 165.</ref>

===Expressionism===
[[Harold Bloom]] describes [[expressionist art]] as attempting to "intensify the expression of feeling and attitude by exaggeration".<ref>Harold Bloom, ''Thomas Hardy'' (2010) p. 93</ref> [[Harold Osborne (writer)|Harold Osborne]] writes that in its wake, even the "new and hard [[New Objectivity|realism]]...kept much of the distortion and exaggeration which had been one of the chief devices of earlier Expressionism".<ref>Harold Osborne ed., ''The Oxford Companion to Art'' (Oxford 1992) p. 397.</ref>

===Tragedy===
[[File:MIles Gloriosus (Grupo Parrocha) (6985293553).jpg|thumb|The "braggart soldier" Pyrgopolynices in a 2012 production of the play ''Miles Gloriosus'']]
Although primarily a comic figure, the boastful ''[[alazon]]'' may be one aspect of the [[tragic]] hero as well: the touch of ''miles gloriosus'' ("braggart soldier") in [[Tamburlaine (play)|Tamburlaine]], even in [[Othello (character)|Othello]], has been commented upon, as has the touch of the obsessed philosopher in [[Faust]]us and [[Prince Hamlet|Hamlet]]'.<ref>Frye, p. 39.</ref>

===Humour===
[[Emil Draitser]] writes that "Some theoreticians of the comic consider exaggeration to be a universal comic device."<ref>Emil Draitser, ''Techniques of Satire'' (1994) p. 135</ref> It may take different forms in different genres, but in the words of M. Eastman and W. Fry, all rely on the fact that 'the easiest way to make things laughable is to exaggerate to the point of absurdity their salient traits'.<ref>M. Eastman/W. Fry, ''Enjoyment of Laughter'' (2008) p. 156.</ref>

A [[caricature]] is a type of [[portrait]] that exaggerates or distorts the essence of a person or thing to create an easily identifiable visual likeness: [[Filippo Baldinucci]] describes this as "disproportionately increasing and emphasizing the defects of the features".<ref>[[Filippo Baldinucci]], quoted in Harold Osborne ed., ''The Oxford Companion to Art'' (Oxford 1992) p. 204.</ref> In literature, a caricature is a description of a person using exaggeration of some characteristics and [[oversimplification]] of others.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://contemporarylit.about.com/cs/literaryterms/g/caricature.htm|title=Literary Term Definition of Resolution|access-date=7 March 2010|archive-date=12 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130112213435/http://contemporarylit.about.com/cs/literaryterms/g/caricature.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Slapstick]] is the recourse to humor involving exaggerated physical activity which exceeds the boundaries of common sense.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thefreedictionary.com/slapstick |title=slapstick – definition of slapstick by the Free Online Dictionary, Thesaurus and Encyclopedia |publisher=Thefreedictionary.com |access-date=2013-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.filmreference.com/encyclopedia/Romantic-Comedy-Yugoslavia/Slapstick-Comedy.html |title=Slapstick Comedy – film, cinema |publisher=Filmreference.com |access-date=2013-04-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/Slapstick+comedy |title=Slapstick comedy definition of Slapstick comedy in the Free Online Encyclopedia |publisher=Encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com |access-date=2013-04-29}}</ref> These exaggerated depictions are often found in cartoons, and light film comedies aimed at younger audiences.

===Overacting===
Overacting is the exaggeration of [[gesture]]s and speech when [[acting]]. It may be unintentional, particularly in the case of a bad [[actor]], or be required for the role. For the latter, it is commonly used in comical situations or to stress the [[evil]] characteristics of a [[villain]]. Since the perception of acting quality differs between people the extent of overacting can be subjective.

Exaggeration is an effect especially useful for [[animation]], as perfect imitation of reality can look static and dull in cartoons.<ref name="AT">{{cite web|url=http://www.animationtoolworks.com/library/article9.html|title=12 Principles|last=Lightfoot|first=Nataha|publisher=Animation Toolworks|access-date=27 June 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160609091550/http://www.animationtoolworks.com/library/article9.html|archive-date=9 June 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The level of exaggeration depends on whether one seeks realism or a particular style, like a caricature or the style of a specific artist. The classical definition of exaggeration, employed by [[Disney]], was to remain true to reality, just presenting it in a wilder, more extreme form.<ref>Johnston & Thomas (1981), pp. 65–66.</ref> Other forms of exaggeration can involve the supernatural or surreal, alterations in the physical features of a character; or elements in the storyline itself.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://wiki.blender.org/index.php/BSoD/Introduction_to_the_Principles_of_Animation/Principles/Exaggeration|title=Exaggeration|last=Willian|date=29 June 2006|publisher=Blender|access-date=28 June 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090207202658/http://wiki.blender.org/index.php/BSoD/Introduction_to_the_Principles_of_Animation/Principles/Exaggeration|archive-date=7 February 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is important to employ a certain level of restraint when using exaggeration.  If a scene contains several elements, there should be a balance in how those elements are exaggerated in relation to each other, to avoid confusing or overawing the viewer.<ref name="PoA E">{{cite web|url=https://www.evl.uic.edu/ralph/508S99/exaggera.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010413033041/http://www.evl.uic.edu/ralph/508S99/exaggera.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=13 April 2001|title=Exaggeration|last=De Stefano|first=Ralph A|publisher=Electronic Visualization Laboratory, [[University of Illinois at Chicago]]|access-date=28 June 2008}}</ref>

===Shock jockery===
A [[shock jock]], a type of [[radio]] broadcaster or [[disc jockey]], entertains listeners or attracts attention using [[humor]] or [[melodrama]]tic exaggeration that some portion of the listening audience may find offensive.

== In journalism ==
[[Arthur Schopenhauer|Schopenhauer]] saw exaggeration as essential to [[journalism]].<ref>
{{cite book | last1 = Schopenhauer | first1 = Arthur | author-link1 = Arthur Schopenhauer | title = Delphi Collected Works of Arthur Schopenhauer | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ajkkDwAAQBAJ| series = Delphi Series Eight | volume = 12| location = Hastings, East Susse | publisher = Delphi Classics | date = 2017 | page = 109 | isbn = 978-1786560889 | access-date = 21 June 2019 | quote =  Exaggeration of every kind is as essential to journalism as it is to the dramatic art; for the object of journalism is to make events go as far as possible. Thus it is that all journalists are, in the very nature of their calling, alarmists; and this is their way of giving interest to what they write.}}</ref>
He may have overstated this case, but [[yellow journalism]] thrived on exaggeration,<ref>
{{cite book | last1 = Griffin | first1 = Brett | title = Yellow Journalism, Sensationalism, and Circulation Wars | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=9vKCDwAAQBAJ | series = The Fourth Estate: Journalism in North America | location = New York | publisher = Cavendish Square Publishing, LLC | date = 2018 | page = 102 | isbn = 978-1502634719 | access-date = 21 June 2019 | quote = yellow journalism[: ...] a style of reporting that relied on exaggerted or invented stories of scandal and crime to attract readers; attention.}}</ref> and [[fact-checking]] and independent verification have not succeeded in suppressing [[clickbait]] or hyperbolic [[headline]]s.

== In politics ==
[[File:John Adams A18236.jpg|thumb|upright|During the election of 1800, surrogates of John Adams' political campaign warned voters that if Thomas Jefferson won the election, "murder, robbery, rape, adultery and incest will openly be taught and practiced."<ref name="Unger">{{cite web |last1=Unger |first1=Rick |title=The Dirtiest Presidential Campaign Ever? Not Even Close! |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/rickungar/2012/08/20/the-dirtiest-presidential-campaign-ever-not-even-close/?sh=6da96db43d84 |work=Forbes |access-date=20 April 2012}}</ref>]]
[[Politician]]s can exaggerate.<ref>
For example:
{{cite book | last1 = Anchimbe | first1 = Eric A. | chapter = Private dialogue in public space: 'Motions of support' letters as response to political action | editor1-last = Berlin | editor1-first = Lawrence N. | editor2-last = Fetzer | editor2-first = Anita | title = Dialogue in Politics | series = Dialogue studies | volume = 18 | location = Amsterdam | publisher = John Benjamins Publishing | date = 2012 | page = 144 | isbn = 978-9027210357| access-date = 21 June 2019 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=G5CeShRyDoMC | quote = Several communicative strategies commonly identified with political discourse produced by politicians can be found in the MoS written by the common people in a bid to represent their voices in the political process in Cameroon. Among these strategies are persuasion, exaggeration, manipulation, vagueness, and falsehood.}}</ref> In the electoral process one may expect exaggeration.<ref>
For example:{{cite book | last1 = Fraser | first1 = Tony | chapter = Trinidad and Tobago | editor1-last = Esipisu | editor1-first = Manoah | editor2-last = Khaguli| editor2-first = Isaac E. | title = Eyes of Democracy: The Media and Elections | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=4_Ju9ZdlwU0C | location = London | publisher = Commonwealth Secretariat | date = 2009 | page = 52 | isbn = 978-0850928983 | access-date = 21 June 2019 | quote = The first requirement of a journalist covering an election in Trinidad and Tobago is to understand the multicultural nature and culture of the people, the disposition to exaggeration of politicians and political parties, the apparent contradictions of the culture and to vow not to take the country's politics too seriously.}}</ref>
Outside, the exaggerations of [[propaganda]]<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Jowett | first1 = Garth | last2 = O'Donnell | first2 = Victoria | chapter = How to Analyze Propaganda | title = Propaganda and Persuasion | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=vIC92PdJ0l0C | edition = 4th | location = Thousand Oaks, California | publisher = Sage Publications | date = 2006 | page = 283 | isbn = 978-1412908986 | access-date = 21 June 2019 | quote = Exaggeration is often associated with propaganda. Goebbels said that outrageous charges evoked more belief than milder statements.}}</ref> can bolster an incumbent's position.

==In psychology==

People with the following mental health issues are prone to make exaggerated representations:
* [[Factitious disorder]]/[[malingering]],<ref name="DSM-5-introduction">{{Cite book |last=American Psychiatric Association |year=2013 |title=Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders |edition=Fifth |publisher=American Psychiatric Publishing |location=Arlington, VA |pages=[https://archive.org/details/diagnosticstatis0005unse/page/5 5–25] |isbn=978-0890425558 |url=https://archive.org/details/diagnosticstatis0005unse/page/5 }}</ref>
* [[Addiction|Substance related and addictive disorders]]
* [[Acute stress disorder]],<ref name="DSM-5-introduction"/>
* [[Post traumatic stress disorder]],<ref name="DSM-5-introduction"/>
* [[Avoidant personality disorder]],<ref name="DSM-5-introduction"/> and
* [[Narcissistic personality disorder]].<ref name="DSM-5-introduction"/>

Factitious disorder is when a person acts as if they have a physical or psychological illness. People with this disorder created the symptoms and are willing to undergo painful or risky tests to get sympathy and special attention.<ref>{{cite web |title=Factitious Disorders |url=https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9832-an-overview-of-factitious-disorders |website=Cleveland Clinic |access-date=2 October 2021}}</ref>

==In popular culture==

In 1969, The [[Monty Python]] [[Dirty Fork]] sketch demonstrates an absurd level of catastrophization where restaurant staff commit suicide and murder each other because of a customer complaint of a dirty fork. Compare with the scene in the film ''[[Monty Python and the Holy Grail]]''<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|last=Sims|first=David|date=2015-04-09|title=How 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail' Influenced Film By Satirizing It|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2015/04/how-monty-python-and-the-holy-grail-influenced-cinema-by-satirizing-it/390195/|access-date=2021-08-31|website=The Atlantic|language=en}}</ref> involving the [[Black Knight (Monty Python)|Black Knight character]] which is the opposite extreme of absurdity ([[Minimisation (psychology)|minimisation]]).<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-05-29|title=Overstatement - Examples and Definition of Overstatement|url=https://literarydevices.net/overstatement/|access-date=2021-08-31|website=Literary Devices|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="auto"/>
